_comment: Provenance for each lesson. Every formula/notation/worked example must trace to a source here. Add an entry per lesson before marking a skill ready. Verify any chapter number against the actual edition; section titles are stable, numbering varies by edition.

rational-holes.title: Vertical asymptotes and holes

sources.section: Rational Functions (vertical asymptotes and removable discontinuities)

conventions: A factor common to numerator and denominator gives a removable discontinuity (hole) at that x; its y is the simplified function evaluated there.
A denominator zero that does not cancel gives a vertical asymptote.
Worked example f(x) = (x+2)(x-1)/((x-1)(x-3)): hole at (1, -1.5), vertical asymptote x = 3, x-intercept (-2, 0).

rational-asymptotes.title: Horizontal and slant asymptotes

sources.section: Rational Functions (horizontal and oblique asymptotes by degree)

conventions: Equal degrees: horizontal asymptote is the ratio of leading coefficients. Example (2x^2+1)/(x^2+1) -> y = 2.
Numerator degree exactly one more than denominator: slant asymptote from the quotient. Example (x^2+1)/x = x + 1/x -> y = x, vertical asymptote x = 0.

rational-graphing.title: Complete rational graphing
conventions: Graph by parts: intercepts, vertical asymptotes, horizontal/slant asymptote, then connect.
Worked example (x^2-1)/(x^2-4): x-intercepts (+/-1, 0), y-intercept (0, 1/4), vertical asymptotes x = +/-2, horizontal asymptote y = 1.

poly-inequalities.title: Polynomial inequalities

sources.section: Rational Functions (sign analysis) and Polynomial Functions

conventions: A polynomial changes sign only at a real zero, so zeros split the line into test intervals.
Test one point per interval; a factor with odd multiplicity flips the sign, even multiplicity does not.
Strict inequality gives open endpoints at the zeros; non-strict includes them.
Worked example p(x) = (x+2)(x-1)(x-3): p > 0 on (-2,1) union (3, infinity).

rational-inequalities.title: Rational inequalities
conventions: Critical points are numerator zeros and denominator zeros; the sign can flip at either.
A value that makes the denominator zero is always excluded, even for a non-strict inequality.
Do not multiply both sides by the denominator: its sign is unknown and could flip the inequality.
Worked example r(x) = (x-3)/(x+1): r > 0 on (-infinity,-1) union (3, infinity); r >= 0 on (-infinity,-1) union [3, infinity).

fta.title: FTA and conjugate root pairs

sources.section: Zeros of Polynomial Functions (Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, Complex Conjugate Theorem)
Complex Zeros; Fundamental Theorem of Algebra

conventions: A degree n polynomial (n >= 1) has exactly n complex roots, counting multiplicity.
With real coefficients, non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs a + bi and a - bi, mirrored across the real axis.
An odd-degree real polynomial has at least one real root.
Worked example p(x) = x^3 - x^2 + 4x - 4 = (x-1)(x^2+4): roots 1, 2i, -2i.

degrees-radians.title: Degree-radian conversion

sources.section: Angles (radian measure, converting between degrees and radians)

conventions: One radian is the central angle subtending an arc equal to the radius; a full turn is 2 pi radians, so 360 degrees = 2 pi and 180 degrees = pi.
Degrees to radians: multiply by pi/180. Radians to degrees: multiply by 180/pi. The unit that cancels tells you the direction.
Worked examples: 120 degrees = 2 pi/3; 5 pi/6 = 150 degrees; 3 pi/4 = 135 degrees.

sum-difference-identities.title: Sum and difference identities
conventions: cos(A +/- B) = cos A cos B -/+ sin A sin B (cosine pairs like with like and flips the sign).
sin(A +/- B) = sin A cos B +/- cos A sin B (sine mixes and keeps the sign).
Worked example cos 75 = cos(45+30) = (sqrt6 - sqrt2)/4; cofunction cos(pi/2 - theta) = sin theta by the difference formula.

double-angle-identities.title: Double-angle identities
conventions: sin 2theta = 2 sin theta cos theta, derived from sin(theta + theta).
cos 2theta = cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta = 2 cos^2 theta - 1 = 1 - 2 sin^2 theta.
Worked example: if sin theta = 3/5 and cos theta = 4/5 then sin 2theta = 24/25.

half-angle-identities.title: Half-angle identities
conventions: sin(theta/2) = +/- sqrt((1 - cos theta)/2); cos(theta/2) = +/- sqrt((1 + cos theta)/2). Derived by solving cos 2alpha for the squared term with alpha = theta/2.
Choose the +/- sign by the quadrant of the half angle theta/2, not of theta.
Worked example sin 22.5 = sin(45/2) = sqrt(2 - sqrt2)/2.

verifying-identities.title: Verifying identities

sources.section: Solving Trigonometric Equations with Identities (verifying identities)

conventions: Transform one side (usually the messier one) into the other; do not move terms across the equals sign as if solving.
Reliable moves: convert to sine and cosine, apply a Pythagorean identity, find a common denominator, split a fraction.
Worked examples: sec theta - cos theta = sin theta tan theta; (1 - cos x)(1 + cos x) = sin^2 x.

unit-circle.title: The unit circle

sources.section: The Unit Circle: Sine and Cosine Functions

conventions: Angle in standard position, counterclockwise positive.
A point on the unit circle at angle theta is (cos theta, sin theta).

vectors.title: Vectors
conventions: Component form v = (v_x, v_y); magnitude |v| = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2).
Direction measured from the positive x-axis, counterclockwise.
Addition drawn tip to tail; subtraction is adding the negative.

polar-graphs.title: Polar graphs
conventions: Point given by (r, theta); x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta.
r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2), theta = arctan(y/x) shown to the learner; the figure computes the angle with a full four-quadrant routine internally.
r = cos(2 theta) traces a four-petaled rose; a negative radius points in the opposite direction.

conics.title: Conics

sources.section: The Ellipse / The Hyperbola / The Parabola

conventions: Standard position at the origin.
Ellipse: sum of distances to two foci is 2a; foci on the major axis.
Hyperbola: absolute difference of distances to two foci is 2a; asymptotes y = +/- (b/a) x.
Parabola: equidistant from focus and directrix.
Eccentricity sorts the family: circle 0, ellipse (0,1), parabola 1, hyperbola >1.

parametrics.title: Parametrics
conventions: A parametric curve gives x and y as functions of a parameter t.
Eliminate the parameter to recover a rectangular relation (line, x^2 + y^2 = 1, etc.).
Lissajous example x = sin 2t, y = sin 3t.

polar-rect.title: Polar-rectangular conversion

sources.section: Polar Coordinates (conversion formulas and non-unique representations)

conventions: Polar to rectangular: x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta (cosine feeds x, sine feeds y).
Rectangular to polar: r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2), theta = arctan(y/x), adding 180 degrees when x < 0 to fix the quadrant.
A point has many polar names: theta + 360 degrees, or negate r and add 180 degrees. Rectangular is unique.
Worked points (3,4) -> (5, 53.13 degrees) and (4, 60 degrees) -> (2, 2 sqrt3).

polar-roses.title: Polar graphs: roses, limacons, cardioids

sources.section: Polar Coordinates: Graphs (rose curves, cardioids, limacons)

conventions: Graph r = f(theta) by sweeping theta and plotting each (r, theta). A negative r plots in the opposite direction.
Rose r = cos(n theta) has n petals when n is odd and 2n petals when n is even.
Cardioid r = 1 + cos theta: max 2 at theta = 0, cusp at the origin where r = 0 at theta = 180 degrees.
Limacon r = a + b cos theta: inner loop when a < b, cardioid when a = b, dimpled for 1 < a/b < 2, convex for a/b >= 2.

param-graph.title: Graphing parametric equations
conventions: Build a table with columns t, x(t), y(t), choose t in increasing order, plot each pair (x, y), then connect in order of increasing t.
Orientation is the direction of travel as t increases, shown with arrows. The parameter t often stands for time.
Worked curve x = t^2 - 1, y = t for -2 <= t <= 2 is a right-opening parabola that fails the vertical line test.

param-elim.title: Eliminating the parameter
conventions: Substitution: solve the simpler equation for t, then substitute into the other. Example x = t + 1, y = t^2 -> y = (x - 1)^2.
Trig method: isolate cos t and sin t, square, and add via cos^2 t + sin^2 t = 1. Example x = 3 cos t, y = 2 sin t -> x^2/9 + y^2/4 = 1.
A restricted range of t keeps only a piece of the full Cartesian curve. Example 0 <= t <= pi gives the upper semicircle y >= 0.

ellipses.title: Ellipses

sources.section: The Ellipse (standard form, vertices vs co-vertices, orientation)

conventions: Standard form x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1. The semi-axes are the square roots of the denominators.
The larger denominator lies under the major axis, so it sets the orientation. Equal denominators give a circle.
Worked example x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1 has a = 5 across and b = 3 up, vertices (+/-5, 0), co-vertices (0, +/-3).

hyperbolas.title: Hyperbolas
conventions: Two standard forms x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 (opens left-right) and y^2/a^2 - x^2/b^2 = 1 (opens up-down).
The positive term sets the opening and holds the vertices at distance a, not the larger denominator.
Worked example x^2/9 - y^2/16 = 1 has vertices (+/-3, 0) and two branches.

eccentricity.title: Foci and eccentricity

sources.section: The Ellipse and The Hyperbola (foci locations and c formulas)

conventions: Ellipse foci: c^2 = a^2 - b^2 (minus, foci inside on the major axis). Hyperbola foci: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 (plus, foci outside beyond the vertices).
Eccentricity e = c/a sorts the family: circle 0, ellipse between 0 and 1, parabola 1, hyperbola greater than 1.
Worked example a = 5, b = 4 gives c = 3 and e = 0.6.

hyp-asym.title: Asymptotes of hyperbolas

sources.section: The Hyperbola (asymptotes and the central rectangle)

conventions: For x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 the asymptotes are y = +/- (b/a) x. For the up-down form they are y = +/- (a/b) x.
The central box has half-widths a and b with corners (+/-a, +/-b), and its diagonals are the asymptotes.
Sketch order: box, diagonals, vertices, branches. Worked example x^2/9 - y^2/16 = 1 has box corners (+/-3, +/-4).
